title: Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019
short_title: Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill changes the Customs Act 1901 so that goods from Peru, Indonesia, and Hong Kong can enter Australia with discounted import taxes.
It sets up rules for identifying which goods count as originating from each of those places and lets regulations require exporters and producers to keep records when they claim those discounts.
Budget papers say the Hong Kong deal would cost the government $40 million in lost revenue over the forecast period, while the Peru and Indonesia deals would have little or no revenue effect.
changes: Creates rules for classifying Peruvian, Indonesian, and Hong Kong goods as eligible for lower customs duty rates.
Allows regulations to impose record-keeping duties on exporters and producers claiming preferential rates.
Works with a separate tariff bill that will list the actual reduced duty rates in the Customs Tariff Act 1995.
summary.affected: Australian exporters and producers of goods shipped to Peru, Indonesia, and Hong Kong, and importers of those goods into Australia.

The amendment was introduced in order to replace a table item 4 in clause 2 of the [Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6426). Senator Steele-John [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2019-11-26.64.1) the amendment related to the Australia-Hong Kong Free Trade Agreement. It would have delayed the commencement of Schedule 3 until the latest of the following dates: > *(a) 20 October 2020;* > > *(b) the day this Act receives the Royal Assent;* > > *(c) the day the Free Trade Agreement between Australia and Hong Kong, China, done at Sydney on 26 March 2019, enters into force for Australia.* > > *However, the provisions do not commence at all if the event mentioned in paragraph (c) does not occur.* > > *The Minister must announce, by notifiable instrument, the day the Agreement enters into force for Australia.* The [explanatory memorandum](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fr6426_ems_8d5f3031-1911-4847-a508-ecf5688cbd98%22;rec=0) explains that: > *Schedule 3 of the Bill amends the Customs Act to provide rules for determining whether goods are Hong Kong originating goods and therefore entitled to be imported into Australia at preferential rates of customs duty. The amendments also enable regulations to prescribe record keeping obligations on exporters and producers of goods exported to Hong Kong, China for which a preferential rate of customs duty is claimed.*

speeches.speaker: Jason Wood
speeches.brief: The bill implements free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, aiming to increase export opportunities and reduce tariffs on Australian goods. The agreements cover 99% of Australian exports to Indonesia duty-free, new quotas for dairy and grains to Peru, and zero tariffs on all goods to Hong Kong, with support from over 30 industry groups.

speeches.speaker: Dave Sharma
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that free trade is essential for Australia's economic prosperity and announced three free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, which will eliminate over 99% of tariffs on Australian goods to Indonesia and Peru and codify existing trade with Hong Kong, aiming to cover 90% of Australia's trade by free trade agreements by 2022.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Labor announced support for the Customs Amendment and Tariff Amendment bills after obtaining written commitments from Trade Minister Simon Birmingham on worker protections, including no new labour market testing waivers, criminal penalties for exploitation, and termination of the 1993 Indonesia bilateral investment treaty. The agreements are expected to boost Australian exports and jobs, with specific benefits for steel, grain, education and manufacturing sectors.

speeches.speaker: Richard Marles
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019, which enables free trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong and Peru, arguing the Indonesia deal is vital given trade is 42% of GDP and Indonesia’s large market. Labor’s second reading amendment, moved by the member for Brand, sought improvements such as labour market testing, protections for working holidaymakers, replacing the 1993 investment treaty’s ISDS clause, and a review of the new clause; the trade minister agreed to most demands in a 21 October response, allowing Labor’s support.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (IA-CEPA) will boost trade and jobs, and announced Labor's support after securing commitments to protect Australian workers, including no additional labour testing waivers, equal treatment for visa holders, and improved investor-state dispute settlement clauses.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019 and related bills, arguing the trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong, and Peru will create jobs and economic growth. The speaker cited four reasons for support: bigger markets mean more jobs, deepening ties with Indonesia is critical, improvements were negotiated on investment protections and labour standards, and engagement with Asia is needed during weak economic growth and global uncertainty.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the free trade agreement with Indonesia, arguing it will eliminate tariffs on grain, cattle, and steel, and create opportunities for Australian vocational education and healthcare providers, while noting that only 2% of Australian exports currently go to Indonesia.

speeches.speaker: Peter Khalil
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Labor supports the free trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong, and Peru, citing recommendations from the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties (JSCOT) including labour market testing protections, termination of the old Indonesia bilateral investment treaty’s survival clause, and independent economic modelling. He also noted that the government should monitor Hong Kong’s autonomous status and that civil society and unions need better consultation in future trade negotiations.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Peru-Australia, Hong Kong, and Indonesia free trade agreements, focusing on the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and noted that Australia exports more to the UK than to Indonesia despite its proximity, with benefits for sectors like steel (BlueScope in Port Kembla) and education, while calling for more Indonesian language study in schools.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Customs Amendment bills for trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong and Peru after the government agreed to demands including retaining labour market testing, modernising investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions, and holding an inquiry into treaty transparency. The speaker also raised concerns about unlicensed electricians and called for stronger enforcement of workplace laws.

speeches.speaker: Bob Katter
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the ignorance of MPs, noting that the previous speaker from Newcastle represents a major coalmining area while the world's biggest coalmining area is in Indonesia.

speeches.speaker: Jason Wood
speeches.brief: The Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implement Australia's obligations under free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, eliminating over 99% of tariffs on Australian goods exports to Indonesia and Peru while guaranteeing existing duty-free access to Hong Kong. The speaker urged Parliament to pass the bills without delay to benefit Australian businesses, exporters, workers, investors, and farmers.
